o: Five philosophers share five forks; philosopher i needs forks i and (i+1)%5 to eat. We must implement `wantsToEat` so that calls from five concurrent threads never deadlock or starve: each call must pick left fork (1), pick right fork (1), eat (3), put right fork (2), put left fork (2) in that order for that philosopher. The judge only checks that the sequence of operations is valid (no two philosophers hold the same fork simultaneously) and that every requested meal completes, so any correct mutual-exclusion scheme works. Since n ≤ 60, performance is irrelevant; correctness under concurrency is everything.
k: Deadlock arises when all philosophers grab one fork and wait forever for the other; breaking symmetry prevents it.
Any scheme that guarantees mutual exclusion on forks and eventual progress is accepted by the judge.
Limiting concurrent diners to 4 (one fewer than forks) trivially guarantees at least one philosopher can always get both forks.

a.i: The simplest correct solution: let only one philosopher execute the entire pick-eat-put sequence at a time by wrapping the whole body in one mutex. This trivially satisfies mutual exclusion and avoids deadlock because no one ever waits while holding a partial set of forks.
s: Create one mutex/lock shared by all threads.
Call pickLeftFork, pickRightFork, eat, putRightFork, putLeftFork in order.
Release the lock so another philosopher can proceed.

c.python:
from threading import Lock

class Solution:
    def __init__(self):
        self.lock = Lock()

    def wantsToEat(self, philosopher, pickLeftFork, pickRightFork, eat, putLeftFork, putRightFork):
        with self.lock:
            pickLeftFork()
            pickRightFork()
            eat()
            putLeftFork()
            putRightFork()

a.t: O(n) total work; each of the 5n calls does constant work, serialized by the lock.
a.sp: O(1) extra space — a single lock.

a.i: Impose a global order on forks: every philosopher picks the lower-numbered fork first, then the higher-numbered one. Philosopher 4 (whose forks are 4 and 0) must pick fork 0 first, breaking the circular wait that causes deadlock. Each fork gets its own mutex, so up to two non-adjacent philosophers can eat concurrently.
s: Give each of the 5 forks its own mutex.
For philosopher i, compute first = min(i, (i+1)%5), second = max(i, (i+1)%5).
Lock the first fork's mutex, then the second's.
Pick both forks, eat, put both down.

c.python:
from threading import Lock

class Solution:
    def __init__(self):
        self.forks = [Lock() for _ in range(5)]

    def wantsToEat(self, philosopher, pickLeftFork, pickRightFork, eat, putLeftFork, putRightFork):
        l, r = philosopher, (philosopher + 1) % 5
        first, second = (l, r) if l < r else (r, l)
        with self.forks[first]:
            with self.forks[second]:
                pickLeftFork()
                pickRightFork()
                eat()
                putLeftFork()
                putRightFork()

a.t: O(n) total work; each meal performs constant lock/unlock operations.
a.sp: O(1) — five fork locks regardless of n.

a.n: Approach 3: Semaphore Limiting Diners to Four (Optimal Concurrency)
a.i: Allow at most four philosophers to compete for forks at once. With four diners and five forks, by pigeonhole at least one philosopher can always acquire both forks, so no deadlock or starvation occurs. This preserves maximum parallelism: non-adjacent philosophers eat simultaneously, unlike Approach 1.
s: Create a counting semaphore initialized to 4 and per-fork mutexes.
On entry, acquire the semaphore (waits if 4 philosophers are already eating/holding forks).
Lock left fork, then right fork; pick both, eat, put both down.
Release the semaphore so a waiting philosopher may proceed.

c.python:
from threading import Semaphore, Lock

class Solution:
    def __init__(self):
        self.seats = Semaphore(4)
        self.forks = [Lock() for _ in range(5)]

    def wantsToEat(self, philosopher, pickLeftFork, pickRightFork, eat, putLeftFork, putRightFork):
        with self.seats:
            with self.forks[philosopher]:
                with self.forks[(philosopher + 1) % 5]:
                    pickLeftFork()
                    pickRightFork()
                    eat()
                    putLeftFork()
                    putRightFork()

a.t: O(n) total work; each meal does constant semaphore and lock operations.
a.sp: O(1) — one semaphore plus five fork locks.

w: In an interview, start with the single-lock solution to establish correctness, then discuss why it kills parallelism and present either the resource-hierarchy ordering or the 4-seat semaphore as an improvement; the semaphore approach is the classic textbook answer and shows the deepest understanding. Common pitfalls: picking forks in inconsistent order (deadlock via circular wait), forgetting to release locks/permits on all paths, and calling `eat` before acquiring both forks. Edge cases: repeated calls for the same philosopher are fine since each invocation fully acquires and releases resources. Follow-ups: generalize to k philosophers and k forks, add fairness/starvation-freedom guarantees (e.g., FIFO semaphores or ticket locks), or handle a philosopher who dies while holding a fork (requires timeouts/leases).
